# tracing - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tracing/^0.1/

## Expand description

A scoped, structured logging and diagnostics system.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

`tracing` is a framework for instrumenting Rust programs to collect
structured, event-based diagnostic information.

In asynchronous systems like Tokio, interpreting traditional log messages can
often be quite challenging. Since individual tasks are multiplexed on the same
thread, associated events and log lines are intermixed making it difficult to
trace the logic flow. `tracing` expands upon logging-style diagnostics by
allowing libraries and applications to record structured events with additional
information about *temporality* and *causality* — unlike a log message, a span
in `tracing` has a beginning and end time, may be entered and exited by the
flow of execution, and may exist within a nested tree of similar spans. In
addition, `tracing` spans are *structured*, with the ability to record typed
data as well as textual messages.

The `tracing` crate provides the APIs necessary for instrumenting libraries
and applications to emit trace data.

*Compiler support:  requires *

`rustc` 1.65+[§](https://docs.rs#core-concepts)Core Concepts

The core of `tracing`’s API is composed of *spans*, *events* and
*subscribers*. We’ll cover these in turn.

[§](https://docs.rs#spans)Spans

To record the flow of execution through a program, `tracing` introduces the
concept of [spans](https://docs.rs/span/index.html). Unlike a log line that represents a *moment in
time*, a span represents a *period of time* with a beginning and an end. When a
program begins executing in a context or performing a unit of work, it
*enters* that context’s span, and when it stops executing in that context,
it *exits* the span. The span in which a thread is currently executing is
referred to as that thread’s *current* span.

For example:

```
use tracing::{span, Level};
let span = span!(Level::TRACE, "my_span");
// `enter` returns a RAII guard which, when dropped, exits the span. this
// indicates that we are in the span for the current lexical scope.
let _enter = span.enter();
// perform some work in the context of `my_span`...
```
The [ span module](https://docs.rs/span/index.html)’s documentation provides further details on how to
use spans.

Warning: In asynchronous code that uses async/await syntax,`Span::enter`may produce incorrect traces if the returned drop guard is held across an await point. See[the method documentation](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#in-asynchronous-code)for details.

[§](https://docs.rs#events)Events

An [ Event](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html) represents a

*moment*in time. It signifies something that happened while a trace was being recorded.

`Event`s are comparable to the log
records emitted by unstructured logging code, but unlike a typical log line,
an `Event` may occur within the context of a span.For example:

```
use tracing::{event, span, Level};
// records an event outside of any span context:
event!(Level::INFO, "something happened");
let span = span!(Level::INFO, "my_span");
let _guard = span.enter();
// records an event within "my_span".
event!(Level::DEBUG, "something happened inside my_span");
```
In general, events should be used to represent points in time *within* a
span — a request returned with a given status code, *n* new items were
taken from a queue, and so on.

The [ Event struct](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html) documentation provides further details on using
events.

[§](https://docs.rs#subscribers)Subscribers

As `Span`s and `Event`s occur, they are recorded or aggregated by
implementations of the [ Subscriber](https://docs.rs/trait.Subscriber.html) trait.

`Subscriber`s are notified
when an `Event` takes place and when a `Span` is entered or exited. These
notifications are represented by the following `Subscriber` trait methods:- `event`- `Event`takes place,
- `enter`- `Span`,
- `exit`- `Span`

In addition, subscribers may implement the [ enabled](https://docs.rs/trait.Subscriber.html#tymethod.enabled) function to

*filter*the notifications they receive based on

[metadata](https://docs.rs/struct.Metadata.html)describing each

`Span`
or `Event`. If a call to `Subscriber::enabled` returns `false` for a given
set of metadata, that `Subscriber` will *not*be notified about the corresponding

`Span` or `Event`. For performance reasons, if no currently
active subscribers express interest in a given set of metadata by returning
`true`, then the corresponding `Span` or `Event` will never be constructed.[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

First, add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
tracing = "0.1"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#recording-spans-and-events)Recording Spans and Events

Spans and events are recorded using macros.

[§](https://docs.rs#spans-1)Spans

The [ span!](https://docs.rs/macro.span.html) macro expands to a

[which is used to record a span. The](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)

`Span` struct[method on that struct records that the span has been entered, and returns a](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.enter)

`Span::enter`[RAII](https://github.com/rust-unofficial/patterns/blob/main/src/patterns/behavioural/RAII.md)guard object, which will exit the span when dropped.

For example:

```
use tracing::{span, Level};
// Construct a new span named "my span" with trace log level.
let span = span!(Level::TRACE, "my span");
// Enter the span, returning a guard object.
let _enter = span.enter();
// Any trace events that occur before the guard is dropped will occur
// within the span.
// Dropping the guard will exit the span.
```
The [ #[instrument]](https://docs.rs/tracing-attributes/latest/tracing_attributes/attr.instrument.html) attribute provides an easy way to
add

`tracing` spans to functions. A function annotated with `#[instrument]`
will create and enter a span with that function’s name every time the
function is called, with arguments to that function will be recorded as
fields using `fmt::Debug`.For example:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use tracing::{Level, event, instrument};
#[instrument]
pub fn my_function(my_arg: usize) {
    // This event will be recorded inside a span named `my_function` with the
    // field `my_arg`.
    event!(Level::INFO, "inside my_function!");
    // ...
}
```
For functions which don’t have built-in tracing support and can’t have
the `#[instrument]` attribute applied (such as from an external crate),
the [ Span struct](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html) has a

[which can be used to easily wrap synchronous code in a span.](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.in_scope)

`in_scope()` methodFor example:

```
use tracing::info_span;
let json = info_span!("json.parse").in_scope(|| serde_json::from_slice(&buf))?;
```
You can find more examples showing how to use this crate [here](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/tree/main/examples).

[§](https://docs.rs#events-1)Events

[ Event](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html)s are recorded using the

[macro:](https://docs.rs/macro.event.html)

`event!````
use tracing::{event, Level};
event!(Level::INFO, "something has happened!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-the-macros)Using the Macros

The [ span!](https://docs.rs/macro.span.html) and

[macros as well as the](https://docs.rs/macro.event.html)

`event!``#[instrument]` attribute
use fairly similar syntax, with some exceptions.[§](https://docs.rs#configuring-attributes)Configuring Attributes

Both macros require a [ Level](https://docs.rs/struct.Level.html) specifying the verbosity of the span or
event. Optionally, the,

[target](https://docs.rs/struct.Metadata.html#method.target)and

[parent span](https://docs.rs/span/struct.Attributes.html#method.parent)may be overridden. If the target and parent span are not overridden, they will default to the module path where the macro was invoked and the current span (as determined by the subscriber), respectively.

For example:

```
span!(target: "app_spans", Level::TRACE, "my span");
event!(target: "app_events", Level::INFO, "something has happened!");
```
```
let span = span!(Level::TRACE, "my span");
event!(parent: &span, Level::INFO, "something has happened!");
```
The span macros also take a string literal after the level, to set the name
of the span (as above).  In the case of the event macros, the name of the event can
be overridden (the default is `event file:line`) using the `name:` specifier.

```
span!(Level::TRACE, "my span");
event!(name: "some_info", Level::INFO, "something has happened!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#recording-fields)Recording Fields

Structured fields on spans and events are specified using the syntax
`field_name = field_value`. Fields are separated by commas.

```
// records an event with two fields:
//  - "answer", with the value 42
//  - "question", with the value "life, the universe and everything"
event!(Level::INFO, answer = 42, question = "life, the universe, and everything");
```
As shorthand, local variables may be used as field values without an
assignment, similar to [struct initializers](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch05-01-defining-structs.html#using-the-field-init-shorthand-when-variables-and-fields-have-the-same-name). For example:

```
let user = "ferris";
span!(Level::TRACE, "login", user);
// is equivalent to:
span!(Level::TRACE, "login", user = user);
```
Field names can include dots, but should not be terminated by them:

```
let user = "ferris";
let email = "ferris@rust-lang.org";
span!(Level::TRACE, "login", user, user.email = email);
```
Since field names can include dots, fields on local structs can be used using the local variable shorthand:

```
let user = User {
    name: "ferris",
    email: "ferris@rust-lang.org",
};
// the span will have the fields `user.name = "ferris"` and
// `user.email = "ferris@rust-lang.org"`.
span!(Level::TRACE, "login", user.name, user.email);
```
Fields with names that are not Rust identifiers, or with names that are Rust reserved words, may be created using quoted string literals. However, this may not be used with the local variable shorthand.

```
// records an event with fields whose names are not Rust identifiers
//  - "guid:x-request-id", containing a `:`, with the value "abcdef"
//  - "type", which is a reserved word, with the value "request"
span!(Level::TRACE, "api", "guid:x-request-id" = "abcdef", "type" = "request");
```
Constant expressions can also be used as field names. Constants
must be enclosed in curly braces (`{}`) to indicate that the *value*
of the constant is to be used as the field name, rather than the
constant’s name. For example:

```
const RESOURCE_NAME: &str = "foo";
// this span will have the field `foo = "some_id"`
span!(Level::TRACE, "get", { RESOURCE_NAME } = "some_id");
```
The `?` sigil is shorthand that specifies a field should be recorded using
its [ fmt::Debug](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html) implementation:

```
#[derive(Debug)]
struct MyStruct {
    field: &'static str,
}
let my_struct = MyStruct {
    field: "Hello world!"
};
// `my_struct` will be recorded using its `fmt::Debug` implementation.
event!(Level::TRACE, greeting = ?my_struct);
// is equivalent to:
event!(Level::TRACE, greeting = tracing::field::debug(&my_struct));
```
The `%` sigil operates similarly, but indicates that the value should be
recorded using its [ fmt::Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) implementation:

```
// `my_struct.field` will be recorded using its `fmt::Display` implementation.
event!(Level::TRACE, greeting = %my_struct.field);
// is equivalent to:
event!(Level::TRACE, greeting = tracing::field::display(&my_struct.field));
```
The `%` and `?` sigils may also be used with local variable shorthand:

```
// `my_struct.field` will be recorded using its `fmt::Display` implementation.
event!(Level::TRACE, %my_struct.field);
```
Additionally, a span may declare fields with the special value [ Empty](https://docs.rs/field/struct.Empty.html),
which indicates that that the value for that field does not currently exist
but may be recorded later. For example:

```
use tracing::{trace_span, field};
// Create a span with two fields: `greeting`, with the value "hello world", and
// `parting`, without a value.
let span = trace_span!("my_span", greeting = "hello world", parting = field::Empty);
// ...
// Now, record a value for parting as well.
span.record("parting", &"goodbye world!");
```
Finally, events may also include human-readable messages, in the form of a
[format string](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/fmt/index.html#usage) and (optional) arguments, **after** the event’s
key-value fields. If a format string and arguments are provided,
they will implicitly create a new field named `message` whose value is the
provided set of format arguments.

For example:

```
let question = "the ultimate question of life, the universe, and everything";
let answer = 42;
// records an event with the following fields:
// - `question.answer` with the value 42,
// - `question.tricky` with the value `true`,
// - "message", with the value "the answer to the ultimate question of life, the
//    universe, and everything is 42."
event!(
    Level::DEBUG,
    question.answer = answer,
    question.tricky = true,
    "the answer to {} is {}.", question, answer
);
```
Specifying a formatted message in this manner does not allocate by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#shorthand-macros)Shorthand Macros

`tracing` also offers a number of macros with preset verbosity levels.
The [ trace!](https://docs.rs/macro.trace.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/macro.debug.html)

`debug!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.info.html)

`info!`[, and](https://docs.rs/macro.warn.html)

`warn!`[behave similarly to the](https://docs.rs/macro.error.html)

`error!`[macro, but with the](https://docs.rs/macro.event.html)

`event!`[argument already specified, while the corresponding](https://docs.rs/struct.Level.html)

`Level`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.trace_span.html)

`trace_span!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.debug_span.html)

`debug_span!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.info_span.html)

`info_span!`[, and](https://docs.rs/macro.warn_span.html)

`warn_span!`[macros are the same, but for the](https://docs.rs/macro.error_span.html)

`error_span!`[macro.](https://docs.rs/macro.span.html)

`span!`These are intended both as a shorthand, and for compatibility with the [ log](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.6/log/)
crate (see the next section).

[§](https://docs.rs#for-log-users)For `log` Users

Users of the [ log](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.6/log/) crate should note that

`tracing` exposes a set of
macros for creating `Event`s (`trace!`, `debug!`, `info!`, `warn!`, and
`error!`) which may be invoked with the same syntax as the similarly-named
macros from the `log` crate. Often, the process of converting a project to
use `tracing` can begin with a simple drop-in replacement.Let’s consider the `log` crate’s yak-shaving example:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use std::{error::Error, io};
use tracing::{debug, error, info, span, warn, Level};
// the `#[tracing::instrument]` attribute creates and enters a span
// every time the instrumented function is called. The span is named after the
// the function or method. Parameters passed to the function are recorded as fields.
#[tracing::instrument]
pub fn shave(yak: usize) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + 'static>> {
    // this creates an event at the DEBUG level with two fields:
    // - `excitement`, with the key "excitement" and the value "yay!"
    // - `message`, with the key "message" and the value "hello! I'm gonna shave a yak."
    //
    // unlike other fields, `message`'s shorthand initialization is just the string itself.
    debug!(excitement = "yay!", "hello! I'm gonna shave a yak.");
    if yak == 3 {
        warn!("could not locate yak!");
        // note that this is intended to demonstrate `tracing`'s features, not idiomatic
        // error handling! in a library or application, you should consider returning
        // a dedicated `YakError`. libraries like snafu or thiserror make this easy.
        return Err(io::Error::new(io::ErrorKind::Other, "shaving yak failed!").into());
    } else {
        debug!("yak shaved successfully");
    }
    Ok(())
}
pub fn shave_all(yaks: usize) -> usize {
    // Constructs a new span named "shaving_yaks" at the TRACE level,
    // and a field whose key is "yaks". This is equivalent to writing:
    //
    // let span = span!(Level::TRACE, "shaving_yaks", yaks = yaks);
    //
    // local variables (`yaks`) can be used as field values
    // without an assignment, similar to struct initializers.
    let _span = span!(Level::TRACE, "shaving_yaks", yaks).entered();
    info!("shaving yaks");
    let mut yaks_shaved = 0;
    for yak in 1..=yaks {
        let res = shave(yak);
        debug!(yak, shaved = res.is_ok());
        if let Err(ref error) = res {
            // Like spans, events can also use the field initialization shorthand.
            // In this instance, `yak` is the field being initalized.
            error!(yak, error = error.as_ref(), "failed to shave yak!");
        } else {
            yaks_shaved += 1;
        }
        debug!(yaks_shaved);
    }
    yaks_shaved
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#in-libraries)In libraries

Libraries should link only to the `tracing` crate, and use the provided
macros to record whatever information will be useful to downstream
consumers.

[§](https://docs.rs#in-executables)In executables

In order to record trace events, executables have to use a `Subscriber`
implementation compatible with `tracing`. A `Subscriber` implements a
way of collecting trace data, such as by logging it to standard output.

This library does not contain any `Subscriber` implementations; these are
provided by [other crates](https://docs.rs#related-crates).

The simplest way to use a subscriber is to call the [ set_global_default](https://docs.rs/subscriber/fn.set_global_default.html)
function:

```
extern crate tracing;
let my_subscriber = FooSubscriber::new();
tracing::subscriber::set_global_default(my_subscriber)
    .expect("setting tracing default failed");
```
```

```
**Warning**: In general, libraries should *not* call
     `set_global_default()`! Doing so will cause conflicts when
     executables that depend on the library try to set the default later.

This subscriber will be used as the default in all threads for the
remainder of the duration of the program, similar to setting the logger
in the `log` crate.

In addition, the default subscriber can be set through using the
[ with_default](https://docs.rs/subscriber/fn.with_default.html) function. This follows the

`tokio` pattern of using
closures to represent executing code in a context that is exited at the end
of the closure. For example:```
let my_subscriber = FooSubscriber::new();
tracing::subscriber::with_default(my_subscriber, || {
    // Any trace events generated in this closure or by functions it calls
    // will be collected by `my_subscriber`.
})
```
This approach allows trace data to be collected by multiple subscribers within different contexts in the program. Note that the override only applies to the currently executing thread; other threads will not see the change from with_default.

Any trace events generated outside the context of a subscriber will not be collected.

Once a subscriber has been set, instrumentation points may be added to the
executable using the `tracing` crate’s macros.

[§](https://docs.rs#log-compatibility)`log` Compatibility

The [ log](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.6/log/) crate provides a simple, lightweight logging facade for Rust.
While

`tracing` builds upon `log`’s foundation with richer structured
diagnostic data, `log`’s simplicity and ubiquity make it the “lowest common
denominator” for text-based logging in Rust — a vast majority of Rust
libraries and applications either emit or consume `log` records. Therefore,
`tracing` provides multiple forms of interoperability with `log`: `tracing`
instrumentation can emit `log` records, and a compatibility layer enables
`tracing` [s to consume](https://docs.rs/trait.Subscriber.html)

`Subscriber``log` records as `tracing` [s.](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html)

`Event`[§](https://docs.rs#emitting-log-records)Emitting `log` Records

This crate provides two feature flags, “log” and “log-always”, which will
cause [spans](https://docs.rs/span/index.html) and [events](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html) to emit `log` records. When the “log” feature is
enabled, if no `tracing` `Subscriber` is active, invoking an event macro or
creating a span with fields will emit a `log` record. This is intended
primarily for use in libraries which wish to emit diagnostics that can be
consumed by applications using `tracing` *or* `log`, without paying the
additional overhead of emitting both forms of diagnostics when `tracing` is
in use.

Enabling the “log-always” feature will cause `log` records to be emitted
even if a `tracing` `Subscriber` *is* set. This is intended to be used in
applications where a `log` `Logger` is being used to record a textual log,
and `tracing` is used only to record other forms of diagnostics (such as
metrics, profiling, or distributed tracing data). Unlike the “log” feature,
libraries generally should **not** enable the “log-always” feature, as doing
so will prevent applications from being able to opt out of the `log` records.

See [here](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags) for more details on this crate’s feature flags.

The generated `log` records’ messages will be a string representation of the
span or event’s fields, and all additional information recorded by `log`
(target, verbosity level, module path, file, and line number) will also be
populated. Additionally, `log` records are also generated when spans are
entered, exited, and closed. Since these additional span lifecycle logs have
the potential to be very verbose, and don’t include additional fields, they
will always be emitted at the `Trace` level, rather than inheriting the
level of the span that generated them. Furthermore, they are categorized
under a separate `log` target, “tracing::span” (and its sub-target,
“tracing::span::active”, for the logs on entering and exiting a span), which
may be enabled or disabled separately from other `log` records emitted by
`tracing`.

[§](https://docs.rs#consuming-log-records)Consuming `log` Records

The [ tracing-log](https://crates.io/crates/tracing-log) crate provides a compatibility layer which
allows a

`tracing` [to consume](https://docs.rs/trait.Subscriber.html)

`Subscriber``log` records as though they
were `tracing` [events](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html). This allows applications using

`tracing` to record
the logs emitted by dependencies using `log` as events within the context of
the application’s trace tree. See [that crate’s documentation](https://docs.rs/tracing-log/latest/tracing_log/#convert-log-records-to-tracing-events)for details.

[§](https://docs.rs#related-crates)Related Crates

In addition to `tracing` and `tracing-core`, the [ tokio-rs/tracing](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing) repository
contains several additional crates designed to be used with the

`tracing` ecosystem.
This includes a collection of `Subscriber` implementations, as well as utility
and adapter crates to assist in writing `Subscriber`s and instrumenting
applications.In particular, the following crates are likely to be of interest:

- `tracing-futures`- `futures`crate, allowing spans to be attached to- `Future`s,- `Stream`s, and- `Executor`s.
- `tracing-subscriber`- `Subscriber`implementations and utilities for working with- `Subscriber`s. This includes a- `FmtSubscriber`- `FmtSubscriber`for logging formatted trace data to stdout, with similar filtering and formatting to the- `env_logger`
- `tracing-log`- `log`- `tracing`- `Event`s within the trace tree. This is useful when a project using- `tracing`have dependencies which use- `log`. Note that if you’re using- `tracing-subscriber`’s- `FmtSubscriber`, you don’t need to depend on- `tracing-log`directly.
- `tracing-appender`

Additionally, there are also several third-party crates which are not
maintained by the `tokio` project. These include:

- `tracing-timing`- `tracing`. It provides a subscriber that records the time elapsed between pairs of- `tracing`events and generates histograms.
- `tracing-opentelemetry`- [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/)-compatible distributed tracing systems.
- `tracing-honeycomb`- [honeycomb.io](https://www.honeycomb.io/). Backed by- `tracing-distributed`
- `tracing-distributed`
- `tracing-actix-web`- `tracing`integration for the- `actix-web`web framework.
- `tracing-actix`- `tracing`integration for the- `actix`actor framework.
- `axum-insights`- `tracing`integration and Application insights export for the- `axum`web framework.
- `tracing-gelf`
- `tracing-coz`- [coz](https://github.com/plasma-umass/coz)causal profiler (Linux-only).
- `tracing-bunyan-formatter`- [bunyan](https://github.com/trentm/node-bunyan)format, enriched with timing information.
- `tracing-wasm`- `Subscriber`/- `Layer`implementation that reports events and spans via browser- `console.log`and- [User Timing API (](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/User_Timing_API).- `window.performance`)
- `tracing-web`- `console.*`and span events to the- [User Timing API (](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/User_Timing_API).- `window.performance`)
- `tide-tracing`- [tide](https://crates.io/crates/tide)middleware to trace all incoming requests and responses.
- `test-log`- `tracing`for tests, based on environment variables with an- `env_logger`compatible syntax.
- `tracing-unwrap`- `Result`or- `Option`types to a- `Subscriber`.
- `diesel-tracing`- `diesel`
- `tracing-tracy`- [Tracy](https://github.com/wolfpld/tracy)profiles in instrumented applications.
- `tracing-elastic-apm`- [Elastic APM](https://www.elastic.co/apm).
- `tracing-etw`- [ETW](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/etw/about-event-tracing)events.
- `tracing-fluent-assertions`- `tracing`spans.
- `sentry-tracing`- [Sentry](https://sentry.io/welcome/).
- `tracing-forest`
- `tracing-loki`- [Grafana Loki](https://grafana.com/oss/loki/).
- `tracing-logfmt`
- `reqwest-tracing`- `reqwest`
- `tracing-cloudwatch`
- `clippy-tracing`- `tracing::instrument`.
- `json-subscriber`- `tracing-subscriber`

If you’re the maintainer of a `tracing` ecosystem crate not listed above,
please let us know! We’d love to add your project to the list!

```

```
**Note**: Some of these ecosystem crates are currently
     unreleased and/or in earlier stages of development. They may be less stable
     than `tracing` and `tracing-core`.

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags)Crate Feature Flags

The following crate [feature flags](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-features-section) are available:

-
A set of features controlling the [static verbosity level](https://docs.rs/level_filters/index.html#compile-time-filters).
-
`log`: causes trace instrumentation points to emit`log``tracing`subscriber has not been set. This is intended for use in libraries whose users may be using either`tracing`or`log`.
-
`log-always`: Emit`log`records from all`tracing`spans and events, even if a`tracing`subscriber has been set. This should be set only by applications which intend to collect traces and logs separately; if an adapter is used to convert`log`records into`tracing`events, this will cause duplicate events to occur.
-
`attributes`: Includes support for the`#[instrument]`attribute. This is on by default, but does bring in the`syn`crate as a dependency, which may add to the compile time of crates that do not already use it.
-
`std`: Depend on the Rust standard library (enabled by default).`no_std`users may disable this feature with`default-features = false`:`[dependencies] tracing = { version = "0.1.38", default-features = false }`

```

```
**Note**: `tracing`'s `no_std` support
     requires `liballoc`.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable Features

These feature flags enable **unstable** features. The public API may break in 0.1.x
releases. To enable these features, the `--cfg tracing_unstable` must be passed to
`rustc` when compiling.

The following unstable feature flags are currently available:

- `valuable`: Enables support for recording- [field values](https://docs.rs/field/index.html)using the- `valuable`

[§](https://docs.rs#enabling-unstable-features)Enabling Unstable Features

The easiest way to set the `tracing_unstable` cfg is to use the `RUSTFLAGS`
env variable when running `cargo` commands:

`RUSTFLAGS="--cfg tracing_unstable" cargo build`Alternatively, the following can be added to the `.cargo/config` file in a
project to automatically enable the cfg flag for that project:

```
[build]
rustflags = ["--cfg", "tracing_unstable"]
```
[§](https://docs.rs#supported-rust-versions)Supported Rust Versions

Tracing is built against the latest stable release. The minimum supported version is 1.65. The current Tracing version is not guaranteed to build on Rust versions earlier than the minimum supported version.

Tracing follows the same compiler support policies as the rest of the Tokio project. The current stable Rust compiler and the three most recent minor versions before it will always be supported. For example, if the current stable compiler version is 1.69, the minimum supported version will not be increased past 1.66, three minor versions prior. Increasing the minimum supported compiler version is not considered a semver breaking change as long as doing so complies with this policy.

# proptest - Rust

## Expand description

This is the reference documentation for the proptest API.

For documentation on how to get started with proptest and general usage
advice, please refer to the [Proptest Book](https://proptest-rs.github.io/proptest/intro.html).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [arbitrary](https://docs.rs/arbitrary/index.html)
- Defines the `Arbitrary`trait and related free functions and type aliases.
- [array](https://docs.rs/array/index.html)
- Support for strategies producing fixed-length arrays.
- [bits](https://docs.rs/bits/index.html)
- Strategies for working with bit sets.
- [bool](https://docs.rs/bool/index.html)
- Strategies for generating `bool`values.
- [char](https://docs.rs/char/index.html)
- Strategies for generating `char`values.
- [collection](https://docs.rs/collection/index.html)
- Strategies for generating `std::collections`of values.
- [num](https://docs.rs/num/index.html)
- Strategies to generate numeric values (as opposed to integers used as bit fields).
- [option](https://docs.rs/option/index.html)
- Strategies for generating `std::Option`values.
- [path](https://docs.rs/path/index.html)- `std`
- Strategies for generating [`PathBuf`] and related path types.
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Re-exports the most commonly-needed APIs of proptest.
- [range_](https://docs.rs/range_subset/index.html)- subset - `std`
- Strategies for generating values by taking samples of index ranges.
- [result](https://docs.rs/result/index.html)
- Strategies for combining delegate strategies into `std::Result`s.
- [sample](https://docs.rs/sample/index.html)
- Strategies for generating values by taking samples of collections.
- [strategy](https://docs.rs/strategy/index.html)
- Defines the core traits used by Proptest.
- [string](https://docs.rs/string/index.html)- `std`
- Strategies for generating strings and byte strings from regular expressions.
- [test_](https://docs.rs/test_runner/index.html)- runner
- State and functions for running proptest tests.
- [tuple](https://docs.rs/tuple/index.html)
- Support for combining strategies into tuples.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_assert.html)- assert
- Similar to `assert!`from std, but returns a test failure instead of panicking if the condition fails.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_assert_eq.html)- assert_ - eq
- Similar to `assert_eq!`from std, but returns a test failure instead of panicking if the condition fails.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_assert_ne.html)- assert_ - ne
- Similar to `assert_ne!`from std, but returns a test failure instead of panicking if the condition fails.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_assume.html)- assume
- Rejects the test input if assumptions are not met.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_compose.html)- compose
- Convenience to define functions which produce new strategies.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_oneof.html)- oneof
- Produce a strategy which picks one of the listed choices.
- [proptest](https://docs.rs/macro.proptest.html)
- Easily define `proptest`tests.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [property_](https://docs.rs/attr.property_test.html)- test - `attr-macro`
- The `property_test`procedural macro simplifies the creation of property-based tests using the`proptest`crate. This macro provides a more concise syntax for writing tests that automatically generate test cases based on properties.

# AdaptiveDecisionKind in krishiv_dataflow::adaptive - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-dataflow/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_dataflow/adaptive/enum.AdaptiveDecisionKind.html

```
pub enum AdaptiveDecisionKind {
    HotKeySplit,
    Repartition,
    SourceThrottle,
    SlowSinkDetected,
}
```
## Expand description

The kind of adaptive decision taken or suppressed.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.HotKeySplit)

### HotKeySplit

A hot key was detected and sub-partition splitting was applied.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Repartition)

### Repartition

The downstream stage partition count was increased due to skew.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.SourceThrottle)

### SourceThrottle

A source was throttled to relieve downstream pressure.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.SlowSinkDetected)

### SlowSinkDetected

A slow sink was detected.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/adaptive.rs.html#282)

# HeavyHittersTracker in krishiv_dataflow::adaptive - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-dataflow/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_dataflow/adaptive/struct.HeavyHittersTracker.html

`pub struct HeavyHittersTracker { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

SpaceSaving top-K frequent-item tracker.

Uses O(K) memory regardless of key cardinality.  Any key appearing in
more than `1/K` fraction of items is guaranteed to be tracked.

Reference: Metwally, Agarwal, Abbadi — “Efficient Computation of Frequent and Top-k Elements in Data Streams” (ICDT 2005).

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/adaptive.rs.html#115-136)#### pub fn [top_k](https://docs.rs#method.top_k)(&self) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[HotKeyReport](https://docs.rs/struct.HotKeyReport.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/adaptive.rs.html#115-136)

#### pub fn [top_k](https://docs.rs#method.top_k)(&self) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[HotKeyReport](https://docs.rs/struct.HotKeyReport.html)>

Return the top-K entries by estimated count, highest first.

    pub max_error: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html),
    pub heat_score: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html),
}## Expand description

A key frequency estimate from the SpaceSaving tracker.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.estimated_count)

`estimated_count: `[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)Estimated occurrence count (may be an overestimate).

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.max_error)

`max_error: `[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)Maximum possible error in the count estimate.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.heat_score)

`heat_score: `[f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html)Heat score: estimated_count / total_items_seen (0.0 – 1.0).

# RateLimiter in krishiv_dataflow::adaptive - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-dataflow/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_dataflow/adaptive/struct.RateLimiter.html

`pub struct RateLimiter { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Token-bucket rate limiter used by `ThrottledSource`.

Replenishes `rows_per_second` tokens per second.  Callers `consume(n)`
tokens and are told how long to wait if the bucket is empty.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/adaptive.rs.html#182-234)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-RateLimiter)### impl [RateLimiter](https://docs.rs/struct.RateLimiter.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/adaptive.rs.html#182-234)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-RateLimiter)

### impl [RateLimiter](https://docs.rs/struct.RateLimiter.html)

Refill tokens based on elapsed time and attempt to consume `n` tokens.

Returns the number of milliseconds the caller should wait before
retrying if the bucket doesn’t have enough tokens, or `None` if the
consumption was satisfied immediately.

# SinkLatencyTracker in krishiv_dataflow::adaptive - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-dataflow/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_dataflow/adaptive/struct.SinkLatencyTracker.html

`pub struct SinkLatencyTracker { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Running statistics for one sink’s write latency.

Uses Welford’s online algorithm for the mean to avoid integer saturation that would occur with a running total on high-frequency sinks.

# StreamingPartitionAdvisor in krishiv_dataflow::adaptive - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-dataflow/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_dataflow/adaptive/struct.StreamingPartitionAdvisor.html

`pub struct StreamingPartitionAdvisor { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

EMA-based partition count advisor for streaming jobs.

Maintains an exponential moving average of observed batch byte sizes and recommends a bucket count derived from that estimate. This lets streaming jobs auto-adapt parallelism without user configuration:

- When batches are large the advisor increases bucket count so no single executor is overwhelmed.
- When batches shrink (e.g., after a source slow-down) the advisor reduces bucket count to avoid unnecessary fan-out overhead.

The recommended count is always clamped to `[min_buckets, max_buckets]`.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Create an advisor.

`initial_buckets` is the starting recommendation before any data is
observed. `alpha` controls how quickly the EMA reacts to new
observations; 0.2 is a reasonable default (5-batch lag).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/adaptive.rs.html#378-381)#### pub fn [with_alpha](https://docs.rs#method.with_alpha)(self, alpha: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/adaptive.rs.html#378-381)

#### pub fn [with_alpha](https://docs.rs#method.with_alpha)(self, alpha: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html)) -> Self

Set the EMA smoothing factor (must be in `(0.0, 1.0]`).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/adaptive.rs.html#387-405)#### pub fn [observe_batch_bytes](https://docs.rs#method.observe_batch_bytes)(&mut self, batch_bytes: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)) -> [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/adaptive.rs.html#387-405)

#### pub fn [observe_batch_bytes](https://docs.rs#method.observe_batch_bytes)(&mut self, batch_bytes: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)) -> [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)

Record one batch observation and return the updated bucket recommendation.

`batch_bytes` is the Arrow memory footprint of the batch
(`RecordBatch::get_array_memory_size()`).

# AggFunction in krishiv_dataflow::aggregate - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-dataflow/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_dataflow/aggregate/enum.AggFunction.html

```
pub enum AggFunction {
    Count,
    Sum,
    Min,
    Max,
    Avg,
    Stddev,
}
```
## Expand description

Supported aggregate functions.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Count)

### Count

Count all rows in the group.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Sum)

### Sum

Sum of an `Int32` or `Int64` column.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Min)

### Min

Minimum of an `Int32` or `Int64` column.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Max)

### Max

Maximum of an `Int32` or `Int64` column.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Avg)

### Avg

Average of numeric columns (`Int32`, `Int64`, `Float64`).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Stddev)

### Stddev

Sample standard deviation (Bessel-corrected, denominator `n-1`) of
numeric columns. Reuses the avg accumulators (`avg_sum` = Σx,
`avg_count` = n) plus `sq_sum` = Σx².

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# AlignmentMode in krishiv_dataflow::barrier_align - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-dataflow/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_dataflow/barrier_align/enum.AlignmentMode.html

```
pub enum AlignmentMode {
    Aligned,
    Unaligned,
}
```
## Expand description

How an operator reacts to checkpoint barriers across its inputs.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Aligned)

### Aligned

Chandy–Lamport **aligned**: block each input as its barrier arrives and
snapshot only once every input has delivered the epoch’s barrier. No
in-flight data is captured, but the wait for the slowest input adds
latency proportional to inter-input skew — the source of p99 checkpoint
spikes under load.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Unaligned)

### Unaligned

**Unaligned**: snapshot immediately when the *first* barrier of an epoch
arrives and never block an input. The operator captures the in-flight
data on the not-yet-barriered inputs (see
[ BarrierAligner::unaligned_capture_inputs](https://docs.rs/struct.BarrierAligner.html#method.unaligned_capture_inputs)) into the checkpoint, so it
is replayed on recovery and exactly-once is preserved

**without**the alignment stall. This is the Flink

`execution.checkpointing.unaligned`
behavior and the key lever for keeping checkpoint latency off the
critical path.## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/barrier_align.rs.html#16)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Copy-for-AlignmentMode)

### impl [Copy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Copy.html) for [AlignmentMode](https://docs.rs/enum.AlignmentMode.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/barrier_align.rs.html#16)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Eq-for-AlignmentMode)

# BarrierAligner in krishiv_dataflow::barrier_align - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-dataflow/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_dataflow/barrier_align/struct.BarrierAligner.html

`pub struct BarrierAligner { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Tracks checkpoint-barrier arrival across an operator’s `num_inputs` input
channels and signals when an epoch is aligned.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Create an **aligned** (Chandy–Lamport) aligner for an operator with
`num_inputs` inputs (clamped to at least one).

Create an **unaligned** aligner: snapshots on the first barrier of each
epoch and never blocks an input.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/barrier_align.rs.html#97-101)#### pub fn [unaligned_capture_inputs](https://docs.rs#method.unaligned_capture_inputs)(&self, triggering_input: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/barrier_align.rs.html#97-101)

#### pub fn [unaligned_capture_inputs](https://docs.rs#method.unaligned_capture_inputs)(&self, triggering_input: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>

In unaligned mode, the input indices whose in-flight data must be
captured into the checkpoint when a barrier on `triggering_input`
triggers the snapshot — every input *except* the one that just delivered
the barrier (its channel is already at the epoch boundary). The operator
serializes those channels’ buffered records into the checkpoint so they
are replayed on recovery. Returns empty for a single-input operator.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/barrier_align.rs.html#109-111)#### pub fn [aligning_epoch](https://docs.rs#method.aligning_epoch)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/barrier_align.rs.html#109-111)

#### pub fn [aligning_epoch](https://docs.rs#method.aligning_epoch)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)>

The epoch currently aligning, if alignment is in progress.

Retains window operator state between continuous streaming drain cycles.

#### pub fn [drain](https://docs.rs#method.drain)(
    &mut self,
    input_batches: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html)>,
) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html)>>

Process newly arrived input batches and return any emitted output.

GAP-15: At the start of each drain cycle we call `purge_expired` on the
underlying window operator.  For non-TTL operators this is a no-op
(returns 0).  For TTL-backed operators it walks all namespaces once and
deletes entries that have passed their `expires_at_ms` timestamp.
This prevents unbounded growth from entries that were written once and
never read again after expiry (lazy-delete alone is insufficient).

Watermark propagation: before eviction, the operator’s TTL state backend
is updated with the watermark computed during the *previous* drain cycle
(`last_watermark_ms`).  This ensures that `purge_expired` uses event time
rather than wall-clock time even for keys that were never read again after
expiry.  Within the batch loop, `set_watermark` is called again after each
watermark advance so that lazy read-time expiry also reflects event time.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/continuous.rs.html#460-554)#### pub fn [drain_transactional](https://docs.rs#method.drain_transactional)(
    &mut self,
    input_batches: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html)>,
) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html)>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/continuous.rs.html#460-554)

#### pub fn [drain_transactional](https://docs.rs#method.drain_transactional)(
    &mut self,
    input_batches: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html)>,
) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html)>>

Process one drain cycle atomically with respect to retained operator state.

The current state and watermark trackers are snapshotted before processing. If any input batch fails, both are restored so callers may retain and retry the same queued input without duplicating partial aggregation state.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/continuous.rs.html#562-575)#### pub fn [tick](https://docs.rs#method.tick)(&mut self, wall_clock_ms: [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i64.html)) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html)>>

Borrow the underlying window spec fields (for diagnostics).
Advance the watermark to `wall_clock_ms` and emit any windows that have
closed due to inactivity, without requiring new row data.

Called by the streaming engine’s idle-tick path (ST-4) so session windows whose inactivity gap has elapsed can close even when the source is quiet.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/continuous.rs.html#591-600)#### pub fn [emit_open_windows_speculative](https://docs.rs#method.emit_open_windows_speculative)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html)>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/continuous.rs.html#591-600)

#### pub fn [emit_open_windows_speculative](https://docs.rs#method.emit_open_windows_speculative)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html)>>

H-14 (audit): speculatively emit currently-open tumbling windows
without mutating the operator state. Returns `None` when the
active operator is not a tumbling window (e.g. session or sliding
windows), or when there are no open windows. The runtime should
call this on a configurable cadence
(`KRISHIV_STREAM_EARLY_FIRE_MS`) and route the snapshot to a
downstream upsert sink keyed on `(key, window_start)`.

Note: this implementation is intentionally minimal — it returns
`None` for the production state-backed window operators, leaving
the primitive available for tests. Wiring it into the
state-backed path requires accessing the underlying non-state
operator through a new accessor on `StateBackedTumblingWindowOperator`,
tracked as a follow-up.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/continuous.rs.html#602-604)

#### pub fn [uses_multi_source_watermark](https://docs.rs#method.uses_multi_source_watermark)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/continuous.rs.html#612-617)#### pub fn [checkpoint](https://docs.rs#method.checkpoint)(&mut self) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/continuous.rs.html#612-617)

#### pub fn [checkpoint](https://docs.rs#method.checkpoint)(&mut self) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

C3: Persist operator state to the state backend for crash recovery.

Delegates to the underlying operator’s `checkpoint()` which writes
accumulated window state to the configured `StateBackend`.  Callers
(the runtime drain loop) should invoke this periodically so that open
windows survive executor restarts.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/continuous.rs.html#626-635)#### pub fn [snapshot](https://docs.rs#method.snapshot)(&mut self) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/continuous.rs.html#626-635)

#### pub fn [snapshot](https://docs.rs#method.snapshot)(&mut self) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)>>

C9: Serialize the current window state to bytes for cross-session persistence.

Calls `checkpoint()` first (writes to the in-memory state backend),
then extracts the state backend’s snapshot bytes. The bytes can be
stored externally (file, etcd, object store) and later restored via
[`restore_from_snapshot`] on a new executor.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/continuous.rs.html#641-648)#### pub fn [peek_snapshot_bytes](https://docs.rs#method.peek_snapshot_bytes)(&self) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/continuous.rs.html#641-648)

#### pub fn [peek_snapshot_bytes](https://docs.rs#method.peek_snapshot_bytes)(&self) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)>>

Serialize state backend contents without running `checkpoint()`.

Use this for read-only observation (e.g. queryable state) where you must not mutate the operator state as a side effect.

Most recently observed watermark, used to restore `last_watermark_ms`
after a snapshot/restore cycle.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/continuous.rs.html#662-677)#### pub fn [restore_from_snapshot](https://docs.rs#method.restore_from_snapshot)(&mut self, bytes: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/continuous.rs.html#662-677)

#### pub fn [restore_from_snapshot](https://docs.rs#method.restore_from_snapshot)(&mut self, bytes: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

C9: Replace the current window state with the contents of a snapshot
previously produced by [`snapshot`].

The watermark is reset to `None` (the executor will advance it on
the first batch). Call this immediately after [`new`] and before any
[`drain`] calls when resuming an executor from a checkpoint.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/continuous.rs.html#686-699)#### pub fn [merge_snapshot](https://docs.rs#method.merge_snapshot)(&mut self, bytes: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/continuous.rs.html#686-699)

#### pub fn [merge_snapshot](https://docs.rs#method.merge_snapshot)(&mut self, bytes: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

Merge an additional snapshot into the current window state additively.

Used after [`restore_from_snapshot`] when this process hosts several
tasks of one job and must union their per-task checkpoint snapshots.
Existing entries are preserved; entries present in `bytes` overwrite
same-key entries (per-task snapshots of the same epoch are disjoint by
key group after a rescaled restore, and identical for duplicated keys).

# GroupStateFn in krishiv_dataflow::group_state - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-dataflow/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_dataflow/group_state/trait.GroupStateFn.html

`pub trait GroupStateFn<S>: `[Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [on_group](https://docs.rs#tymethod.on_group)(
        &mut self,
        key: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
        rows: &[(&[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html), [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html))],
        state: &mut [GroupState](https://docs.rs/struct.GroupState.html)<S>,
    ) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html)>>;
}## Expand description

User-defined function called **once per group per micro-batch**.

Implement this trait to process all rows for a single key together —
equivalent to Spark’s `mapGroupsWithState` / `flatMapGroupsWithState`.

`S` is the per-group state type.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/group_state.rs.html#121-126)#### fn [on_group](https://docs.rs#tymethod.on_group)(
    &mut self,
    key: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
    rows: &[(&[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html), [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html))],
    state: &mut [GroupState](https://docs.rs/struct.GroupState.html)<S>,
) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html)>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/group_state.rs.html#121-126)

#### fn [on_group](https://docs.rs#tymethod.on_group)(
    &mut self,
    key: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
    rows: &[(&[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html), [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html))],
    state: &mut [GroupState](https://docs.rs/struct.GroupState.html)<S>,
) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html)>>

Process all rows for `key` in the current micro-batch.

- `key`— the group’s key string (derived from the key column).
- `rows`— slice of- `(batch, row_index)`pairs;- **empty**when called for a timeout expiry.
- `state`— mutable per-group state. Call- `state.update(…)`to persist state for the next batch, or- `state.remove_state()`to drop it.

Returns output [ RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html)es emitted by this invocation (may be empty).

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# OperatorConfig in krishiv_dataflow::operator_config - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-dataflow/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_dataflow/operator_config/struct.OperatorConfig.html

```
pub struct OperatorConfig {
    pub uid:
```
[OperatorUid](https://docs.rs/struct.OperatorUid.html),
    pub parallelism: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
    pub max_parallelism: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
    pub behavior_version: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html),
}## Expand description

Per-operator execution configuration.

Holds the parallelism settings and the stable UID required for savepoint
compatibility. The `behavior_version` field is used by the incremental
computing layer: bumping it signals that the operator’s logic has changed,
causing any cached `Trace` state to be discarded and recomputed from scratch.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.uid)

`uid: `[OperatorUid](https://docs.rs/struct.OperatorUid.html)Stable UID used to match state in savepoints and incremental Traces.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.parallelism)

`parallelism: `[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)Actual degree of parallelism (`1` means no key partitioning).

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.max_parallelism)

`max_parallelism: `[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)Maximum parallelism determines the key-space partitioning granularity.

This value must not change across savepoint restores.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.behavior_version)

`behavior_version: `[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)Incremental computing: bump this when the operator’s UDF or transformation
logic changes. The `LogicFingerprint` is derived from `(uid, behavior_version)`.
When the fingerprint changes, the cached incremental `Trace` for this
operator is invalidated and recomputed from scratch. Default: `0`.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Create a new `OperatorConfig` with the given UID and default parallelism.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/operator_config.rs.html#90-93)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/operator_config.rs.html#99-102)#### pub fn [with_behavior_version](https://docs.rs#method.with_behavior_version)(self, v: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)) -> Self

#### pub fn [with_behavior_version](https://docs.rs#method.with_behavior_version)(self, v: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)) -> Self

Set the behavior version for incremental Trace cache invalidation.

Bump this (e.g., `0` → `1`) when UDF logic changes so that previously
cached incremental results are discarded and recomputed correctly.

# OperatorUid in krishiv_dataflow::operator_config - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-dataflow/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_dataflow/operator_config/struct.OperatorUid.html

`pub struct OperatorUid(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

A stable string identifier for a streaming operator.

Survives job restarts and is used to correlate operator state in savepoints. Two operators with the same UID in topologically equivalent positions will share state across a restart.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

# execute_bounded_window in krishiv_dataflow::operator_runtime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-dataflow/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_dataflow/operator_runtime/fn.execute_bounded_window.html

```
pub fn execute_bounded_window(
    input_batches:
```
[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html)>,
    spec: &[WindowExecutionSpec](https://docs.rs/krishiv-plan/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/krishiv_plan/window/struct.WindowExecutionSpec.html),
    state_dir: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<&[Path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html)>,
) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html)>>## Expand description

Execute a bounded windowed stream over in-memory batches (canonical semantics).

Watermark advances to the max event time per input batch, then the whole batch
is passed to the window operator (see `streaming-execution-model.md`).

`state_dir` controls where the operator’s window state is persisted:

- `Some(dir)`: state lives under- `dir/{window_kind}/`and survives process restarts. Required for exactly-once semantics across multiple bounded window invocations against the same key space (e.g. an executor’s- `state:store:`fragment).
- `None`: state is ephemeral (in a- `tempdir`) and lives only for the duration of this call. Suitable for one-shot batch SQL where the operator’s state does not need to outlive the call.

---

# execute_window_join in krishiv_dataflow::operator_runtime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-dataflow/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_dataflow/operator_runtime/fn.execute_window_join.html

```
pub fn execute_window_join(
    left_batches: &[
```
[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html)],
    right_batches: &[[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html)],
    spec: [WatermarkWindowJoinSpec](https://docs.rs/watermark_join/struct.WatermarkWindowJoinSpec.html),
    final_watermark_ms: [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i64.html),
) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html)>>## Expand description

ST8: Execute a stream-stream watermark-bounded window join over pre-collected batches.

Routes left and right batches (interleaved by index) through a
[`WatermarkWindowJoinOperator`].  After processing, calls
`advance_watermark(final_watermark_ms)` to flush any remaining state.
Returns joined `RecordBatch`es (left cols ∥ right cols, with `left_` /
`right_` prefixes when column names collide).

---

# execute_window_join_aligned in krishiv_dataflow::operator_runtime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-dataflow/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_dataflow/operator_runtime/fn.execute_window_join_aligned.html

```
pub fn execute_window_join_aligned(
    spec:
```
[WatermarkWindowJoinSpec](https://docs.rs/watermark_join/struct.WatermarkWindowJoinSpec.html),
    events: impl [IntoIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.IntoIterator.html)<Item = [JoinStreamEvent](https://docs.rs/enum.JoinStreamEvent.html)>,
    final_watermark_ms: [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i64.html),
) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[AlignedJoinOutput](https://docs.rs/struct.AlignedJoinOutput.html)>## Expand description

Drive a windowed join continuously, taking a consistent snapshot each time a
checkpoint barrier **aligns** across both inputs (Chandy–Lamport).

This is the multi-input counterpart of the single-operator continuous loop:
the [`WatermarkWindowJoinOperator`]’s [ BarrierAligner](https://docs.rs/barrier_align/struct.BarrierAligner.html)
blocks the input that delivered a barrier first — buffering its post-barrier
batches — until the other input’s barrier arrives. On alignment the operator
is snapshotted and the buffered batches are replayed into the next epoch, so
no input is dropped or double-counted across the checkpoint boundary.

---

}## Expand description

User-defined per-key processing function.

Implement this trait to build stateful stream operators that are not covered by the built-in window operators.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

#### fn [on_event](https://docs.rs#tymethod.on_event)(
    &mut self,
    key: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
    batch: &[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html),
    row: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
    ctx: &mut [ProcessContext](https://docs.rs/struct.ProcessContext.html)<'_>,
) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

Process one row from an input batch.

`key` is the serialised join key. `batch` is the full input batch;
`row` is the row index within it.

The function may read and write `ctx.state` and call `ctx.emit` and
`ctx.register_event_time_timer` / `ctx.register_processing_time_timer`.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/process_fn.rs.html#128-133)#### fn [on_timer](https://docs.rs#tymethod.on_timer)(
    &mut self,
    key: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
    fire_time_ms: [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i64.html),
    ctx: &mut [ProcessContext](https://docs.rs/struct.ProcessContext.html)<'_>,
) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/process_fn.rs.html#128-133)

#### fn [on_timer](https://docs.rs#tymethod.on_timer)(
    &mut self,
    key: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
    fire_time_ms: [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i64.html),
    ctx: &mut [ProcessContext](https://docs.rs/struct.ProcessContext.html)<'_>,
) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

Called when a timer fires (watermark ≥ `fire_time_ms` for event-time
timers, or processing_time ≥ `fire_time_ms` for processing-time timers).

The function may emit output and register new timers.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/process_fn.rs.html#412-434)#### pub fn [restore](https://docs.rs#method.restore)(&mut self, bytes: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/process_fn.rs.html#412-434)

#### pub fn [restore](https://docs.rs#method.restore)(&mut self, bytes: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [ExecResult](https://docs.rs/type.ExecResult.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

Restore operator state and pending timers from a snapshot blob.

The `ProcessFunction` itself is not serialised; only state and timers
are restored. Multiple task snapshots can be merged by calling
`restore` repeatedly — state keys from later calls overwrite earlier
ones, and timers are merged idempotently.

# TimerKind in krishiv_dataflow::process_fn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-dataflow/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_dataflow/process_fn/enum.TimerKind.html

```
pub enum TimerKind {
    EventTime,
    ProcessingTime,
}
```
## Expand description

Discriminates between event-time and processing-time timers.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.EventTime)

### EventTime

Fires when the event-time watermark reaches `fire_time_ms`.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ProcessingTime)

### ProcessingTime

Fires when the wall-clock processing time reaches `fire_time_ms`.

# OperatorMessage in krishiv_dataflow::queue - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-dataflow/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_dataflow/queue/enum.OperatorMessage.html

```
pub enum OperatorMessage {
    Data(
```
[RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html)),
    Barrier {
        epoch: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html),
    },
}## Expand description

A message that can travel through an `OperatorQueue`.

Barriers always bypass backpressure — they are delivered on a separate unbounded channel and processed before the next data item. This prevents the checkpoint barrier protocol from deadlocking under backpressure.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Data)

### Data([RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/arrow-array/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_array/record_batch/struct.RecordBatch.html))

A record batch from the operator’s output.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Barrier)

### Barrier

A checkpoint barrier for epoch `epoch`.

`len: `[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)Number of items currently in the data queue.

`unaligned_dropped: `[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)Total number of in-flight records that were dropped because the unaligned buffer was full. Counters are monotonically increasing for the lifetime of the queue.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.unaligned)

`unaligned: `[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)Whether the queue is in unaligned mode.

# OperatorQueueReceiver in krishiv_dataflow::queue - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-dataflow/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_dataflow/queue/struct.OperatorQueueReceiver.html

`pub struct OperatorQueueReceiver { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Receiving half of an `OperatorQueue`.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/queue.rs.html#244-320)#### pub async fn [recv](https://docs.rs#method.recv)(&mut self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[OperatorMessage](https://docs.rs/enum.OperatorMessage.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/queue.rs.html#244-320)

#### pub async fn [recv](https://docs.rs#method.recv)(&mut self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[OperatorMessage](https://docs.rs/enum.OperatorMessage.html)>

Receive the next message.

Priority order:

- Buffered in-flight records (unaligned mode only) — drained first so the snapshot metadata captures the exact set of in-flight records the operator saw.
- Barrier epochs stored in `pending_barriers`(deferred from previous calls where data and barriers arrived simultaneously), drained FIFO.
- All barriers currently available on `barrier_rx`(drained before blocking).
- The next data batch from `data_rx`(async wait). Any barriers that arrive while waiting are queued in`pending_barriers`and returned on subsequent calls — before the next data item.

In unaligned mode, records that arrive after a barrier and before
the next barrier are *held* in the in-flight buffer (not delivered
to the operator) so the snapshot can record them. When the next
barrier arrives, the buffer is drained back to the operator in
FIFO order — so the operator sees those records only after the
barrier. This is the unaligned-checkpoint contract: the operator
makes progress, but the data plane and the control plane see
records at slightly different points so the snapshot is complete.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/queue.rs.html#328-340)#### pub fn [drain_unaligned_buffer](https://docs.rs#method.drain_unaligned_buffer)(&mut self) -> ([Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[BufferedBatch](https://docs.rs/type.BufferedBatch.html)>, [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/queue.rs.html#328-340)

#### pub fn [drain_unaligned_buffer](https://docs.rs#method.drain_unaligned_buffer)(&mut self) -> ([Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[BufferedBatch](https://docs.rs/type.BufferedBatch.html)>, [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html))

Drain the unaligned-mode in-flight buffer. Used by the snapshot logic to capture the exact set of records the operator saw between the last barrier and now.

Returns the records (FIFO) and the lifetime dropped-count at the moment of the snapshot.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/queue.rs.html#343-345)#### pub fn [unaligned_buffer_len](https://docs.rs#method.unaligned_buffer_len)(&self) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/krishiv_dataflow/queue.rs.html#343-345)

#### pub fn [unaligned_buffer_len](https://docs.rs#method.unaligned_buffer_len)(&self) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

Current number of buffered in-flight records (unaligned mode).

# operator_queue in krishiv_dataflow::queue - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-dataflow/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_dataflow/queue/fn.operator_queue.html

```
pub fn operator_queue(
    capacity:
```
[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
) -> ([OperatorQueueSender](https://docs.rs/struct.OperatorQueueSender.html), [OperatorQueueReceiver](https://docs.rs/struct.OperatorQueueReceiver.html))## Expand description

Create a bounded operator queue with `capacity` data slots in
`Aligned` mode (the default).

Barriers use an unbounded channel so they always bypass backpressure, preventing checkpoint-protocol deadlock. This matches the module-level contract: “Barriers always bypass backpressure — they are delivered on a separate unbounded channel.”

---

# StateValue in krishiv_dataflow::state_descriptor - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-dataflow/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_dataflow/state_descriptor/trait.StateValue.html

```
pub trait StateValue:

```
[Serialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html)
    + [DeserializeOwned](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.DeserializeOwned.html)
    + [Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html) { }## Expand description

Marker trait for types that can be stored as operator state.

Any type that is `Serialize + DeserializeOwned + Default` automatically
qualifies. Implement this for your domain types or use the blanket impl.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

`window_ms: `[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)Half-width of the join window in milliseconds.  Left event `L` matches
right event `R` when `R.ts ∈ [L.ts − window_ms, L.ts + window_ms]`.
